# Session 6 · Analyse: from sample to answer

## Week 6 · Saturday

- Recap quiz on Session 5 (10 min)
- 6.1 From sample to population: CI, p-value, one- or two-sided, power, sample size, choosing a test
- 6.2 Compare groups in the course dataset (live R demo)
- 6.3 Relationships and models: regression, Kaplan-Meier and Cox
- 6.4 Model the course dataset: adjusted OR, Cox HR, missing data, the SAP
- Proposal builder 6: sample size, analysis plan, missing-data plan

::: {.notes}
Session 6 (19:30-22:30, break 20:40-20:55). The most technical session: go slowly and drop extra slides, but never the checks.

FLUID-ICU returns in 6.2 (comparisons) and 6.4 (models, survival, missing data): Q1 in full, Q2 to Q5 briefly.

At the end, each participant chooses one question for the Results section and receives the manuscript brief.
:::

## Recap quiz: Session 5 in three questions

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 10 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Q1. ICU length of stay in 300 patients is right-skewed. Which summary goes in Table 1?
- Q2. A CRF item reads 'Lactate: \_\_\_\_'. Name two things missing.
- Q3. In the raw FLUID-ICU data, one age was 210. Which check catches it, and what goes in the cleaning log?
- Q1 in a poll. Q2 and Q3: two or three people answer with the microphone on (1 to 2 minutes each)
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone back on track with data types, CRF items and cleaning
:::

::: {.notes}
Recap (19:30-19:40). First read three or four Session 5 exit answers and correct misunderstandings.

Q1 as a poll, Q2 and Q3: call on two or three people. The answers are on the next slide.
:::

## Recap quiz: answers

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Q1. ICU stay]{.neu-card-title}

- Median (IQR)
- The data are skewed
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Q2. Lactate item]{.neu-card-title}

- The unit (mmol/L)
- The time point
- A 'not done' option
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Q3. Age 210]{.neu-card-title}

- A range check
- Log: ID, value, correction, reason, who and when
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Skewed: median (IQR). Every CRF item needs a unit and a time. Every correction goes in the log.
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers (1 minute). Read each answer and its reason. Correct the misunderstandings seen in the poll and the chat.
:::

## 6.1 From sample to population, without fear

:::: {.neu-statement}
::: {.neu-big}
We study a few patients to learn about many.
:::

::: {.neu-sub}
6.1 From sample to population  \|  40 minutes
:::
::::

::: {.notes}
Section 6.1 (19:40-20:20).

We study a sample and use statistics to say how far our answer might be from the truth.

Reassure: reading CIs and p-values correctly is more than many published authors manage.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** About 95 of 100 such intervals capture the truth. We never know which ones.
:::

::: {.notes}
The most important picture tonight. Same study 20 times, 25 patients each: 19 intervals contain the true value, one misses. That is what '95%' means.

In real life you see one interval and never the dashed line.

Safe wording: 'a range of plausible values'.

Ask: what makes intervals shorter? Expected: more patients, less variability.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** p = how often chance alone would give a result at least as far from 0 as ours.
:::

::: {.notes}
Walk the three steps on the right. 1: suppose A and B do not differ (H0). 2: repeat the study many times and chance alone spreads the results around 0. 3: p is the share of those repeats at least as far from 0 as our result, on either side: the orange area.

p = 0.04: surprising if there were no difference. p = 0.42 (Paper 1): not surprising, but not proof of no difference.

0.05 is a convention: 0.049 and 0.051 are the same evidence.
:::

## One-sided or two-sided? Two-sided is the default

::: {.neu-intro}
H0 (null hypothesis): no difference. H1 (alternative hypothesis): there is a difference. The direction of H1 decides which tails count.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Two-sided (the default)]{.neu-card-title}

- H1: the groups differ, in either direction
- A difference either way counts: fewer or more deaths
- The p-value uses both tails
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
[One-sided (only if planned)]{.neu-card-title}

- H1: one direction only, e.g. 'restrictive is better'
- Needs a strong reason, written before the data
- Same data give about half the p-value
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Do not confuse with non-inferiority]{.neu-card-title}

- Non-inferiority asks: is the new treatment not worse by more than a margin?
- That is a trial design (Session 3), not a choice of p-value
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Two-sided is the default. One-sided is fine only if stated in advance with a reason.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two-sided is the default: a difference in either direction counts. Paper 1 and the FLUID-ICU SAP use two-sided tests.

One-sided halves the p-value. It is acceptable when it is stated in advance, with a reason to expect only one direction. Switching after seeing results is p-hacking.

The third card prevents a common mix-up: 'one direction' is not the same as a non-inferiority trial, which tests whether a new treatment is not worse by more than a set margin.

Poll: 'one-sided p = 0.03' with no reason. Convinced? Expected: no.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Five common p-value mistakes

::: {.neu-intro}
Each of these sentences appears in published papers. All are wrong. (H0 = the null hypothesis: no difference.)
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:5"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
['Chance of H0']{.neu-card-title}

- p is not the chance that the intervention has no effect
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
['Big effect']{.neu-card-title}

- A small p is not a big or important effect
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
['Not effective']{.neu-card-title}

- p \> 0.05 does not prove the intervention is not effective
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
['A trend']{.neu-card-title}

- p = 0.08 is not 'almost significant'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
['Only p']{.neu-card-title}

- p alone is not enough
- Give the effect and its 95% CI
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Report the effect size with its 95% confidence interval. The p-value is a supporting actor.
:::

::: {.notes}
1: p assumes H0, it is not its probability. 2: a tiny p can come with a trivial effect if the effect is estimated precisely (i.e. when the sample size is large). 3: Paper 1, p = 0.42 with a wide CI means 'we do not know': absence of evidence, not evidence of absence. 4: no 'trend'. 5: give the effect and its CI, as Paper 2 does (HR 2.13, 1.48-3.06).

Also in Exercise 1.
:::

## Check your understanding: CI and p-value

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 3 min
:::

::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- 'Hazard ratio (HR) 2.13, 95% confidence interval (CI) 1.48 to 3.06': the data are compatible with a true HR from about 1.5 to 3.1. True or false?
- 'p = 0.42, so the two strategies are equivalent.' True or false?
- 'p = 0.03 means a 3% chance that there is no effect.' True or false?
- 'A larger study usually gives a narrower CI.' True or false?
- Answer each one in the poll
:::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone can read a CI and avoid the classic p-value mistakes
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (3 minutes), one true/false poll each. Show the results, then the answer slide.
:::

## Answers: CI and p-value

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Statement 1: true]{.neu-card-title}

- The 95% CI is the range of plausible values for the true HR
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Statement 2: false]{.neu-card-title}

- Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence: we do not know
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Statement 3: false]{.neu-card-title}

- p assumes there is no effect, so it cannot be the chance of no effect
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Statement 4: true]{.neu-card-title}

- More patients give a more precise estimate, a narrower CI
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Read the 95% confidence interval first. p never tells you the chance that there is no effect.
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers (1 minute). If the class split on 2 or 3, go back to the p-value picture.
:::

## Type I and type II errors: the fire alarm

| There is a fire (real effect) | No fire (no real effect) |
|:---|:---|
| Alarm rings (p \< 0.05, 'significant') | Correct alarm: power (aim for 80-90%) | False alarm: type I error (alpha, usually 5%) |
| Alarm silent (p of 0.05 or more) | Missed fire: type II error (beta) | Correctly quiet |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Alpha = risk of a false alarm. Power = chance of detecting a real effect. A less sensitive alarm (smaller alpha) gives fewer false alarms but more missed fires, unless you buy a better alarm: more patients.
:::

::: {.notes}
A test is a fire alarm. Type I error: false alarm (alpha, 5%). Type II error: missed fire (beta). Power: the alarm rings when there is a fire (aim 80-90%).

A small 'negative' trial may be a missed fire: Paper 1 was a pilot.

Ask: which error is worse for an expensive, risky drug? For a cheap, safe one?

The next slide shows why a smaller alpha raises beta, and why more patients lower it.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A smaller alpha costs power. More patients buy it back.
:::

::: {.notes}
The fire alarm as areas (2 minutes). Grey curve: results if there is no effect. Teal curve: results if the effect is real. The dashed line is the cut-off for 'significant'.

A: alpha 5%, beta 20%, power 80%. B: a stricter alpha (1%) moves the line right, so more real effects fall left of it: beta rises to 41%. C: twice the patients make both curves narrower, so they overlap less: beta falls to 2%.

This is why sample size is calculated from alpha, power, the effect and the SD.
:::

## Sample size: bigger effect, less variability = fewer patients

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Sample size depends on the effect you hope to detect and on how much patients vary (SD).
:::

::: {.notes}
Fewer patients are needed when the difference is bigger and patients vary less.

Halve the difference: about four times the patients.

Paper 1: 70 vs 40 ml/kg, SD 35, 80% power: 22 per group, 50 in total with deaths.

The expected effect comes from earlier studies or the smallest difference that would change practice.
:::

## Live demo: an online sample-size calculator

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#B5651D"}
LIVE DEMO · 5 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#B5651D"}
- Open a free online calculator (for example OpenEpi) on the shared screen
- Two means: 70 vs 40 ml/kg, SD (standard deviation) 35, power 80%, alpha 5%: 22 per group
- Two proportions: mortality 40% vs 30%: about 356 per group
- Change one input at a time. Predict the direction first (poll)
- Offline fallback: the Neudata sample-size spreadsheet
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#B5651D"}
What changes n?

- Smaller effect: n goes up
- More variability (SD): n goes up
- More power: n goes up
- Add 10-20% for drop-outs
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#B5651D"}
**OUTPUT** Everyone has seen how the effect, the SD, power and alpha change the number of patients
:::

::: {.notes}
Live demo, 5 minutes. Script: s6\_demo.md, Part A.

Reproduce Paper 1 (70 vs 40, SD 35): 22 per group. Then mortality 40% vs 30%: about 356 per group.

Change one input at a time and poll the direction first.

Offline: the sample-size spreadsheet. Participants watch and predict, they do not calculate.
:::

## Choosing a test: one decision table

| Outcome | Shape or counts | Two independent groups | Same patients twice (paired) |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Continuous variable | Roughly symmetric | t-test | Paired t-test |
| Continuous variable | Skewed, or small sample | Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) | Wilcoxon signed-rank |
| Binary variable (yes/no): compare two proportions | Expected counts 5 or more | Chi-square | McNemar |
| Binary variable (yes/no): compare two proportions | Small counts (under 5) | Fisher's exact test | McNemar |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Outcome type + shape + paired or not = the right test. We use the two-group column in this course. The paired tests (Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar) are for reference.
:::

::: {.notes}
Two questions choose the test: continuous or binary, then shape or counts. Paired data use the last column, which we only name.

The last two rows compare two proportions, e.g. 18% vs 36% dying. Paper 1 used the Wilcoxon rank-sum (Mann-Whitney U) test because fluid balance is skewed.

Three or more groups: mention ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis only.

Ask: AKI in 24 vs 24 patients, 3 and 7 events? Expected: Fisher's exact.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Same patients measured twice = paired test. Different patients = unpaired.
:::

::: {.notes}
Same 20 patients: as two clouds the change is hidden, joined as pairs every line goes down. Each patient is their own control.

Common mistake: an unpaired test on before/after data.

Ask: pain scores before and after a new protocol in 30 patients? Expected: paired.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Multiple comparisons: the jelly-bean problem

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.neu-side-notes}
### What to do

- Follow the analysis plan (SAP) written before seeing the data
- Pre-specify one primary outcome
- Label the rest as exploratory
- Adjust, e.g. Bonferroni: 0.05 / number of tests
- Report every test you ran
:::
:::

:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Test 20 things and one will be 'significant' by chance alone.
:::

::: {.notes}
Test 20 colours with no real effect and one comes out at p = 0.03. With 20 tests the chance of at least one false alarm is about 64%.

Remedies: stick to the SAP written before looking at the data, one pre-specified primary outcome, the rest exploratory, Bonferroni if needed, report every test.

Ask: 12 subgroups, one with p = 0.04. Convinced? Expected: not very.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

If R fails, use the next slide.

## FLUID-ICU: four outcomes, four comparisons

| Outcome (type) | Negative balance (n = 245) | Positive balance (n = 373) | Test | Result |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| 28-day death (yes/no) | 45 (18.4%) | 134 (35.9%) | Chi-square | Risk difference 17.6 points (95% CI 10.7 to 24.4), p \< 0.001 |
| Acute kidney injury (yes/no) | 71 (29.0%) | 230 (61.7%) | Chi-square | Risk difference 32.7 points (95% CI 25.2 to 40.2), p \< 0.001 |
| Ventilator-free days (0-28, skewed) | Median 28 (22 to 28) | Median 20 (0 to 28) | Wilcoxon rank-sum | Difference\* -3.0 days (95% CI -5.0 to 0.0), p \< 0.001 |
| ICU stay in survivors (days, skewed) | 4.8 (3.3 to 7.1), n = 200 | 7.5 (5.2 to 11.2), n = 239 | Wilcoxon rank-sum | Difference\* 2.5 days (95% CI 1.8 to 3.2), p \< 0.001 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
n (%) or median (IQR). Positive minus negative group. \*Hodges-Lehmann difference: the median of all differences between a patient of one group and a patient of the other, not the difference between the two medians. All from 03\_compare.R.
:::

::: {.notes}
One test per outcome type, each result read as an effect with its 95% CI, all made by 03\_compare.R.

Death (Q1): risk difference 17.6 points (10.7 to 24.4). AKI (Q2): 32.7 points (25.2 to 40.2). Ventilator-free days (Q3): -3.0 days (-5.0 to 0.0). ICU stay in survivors (Q5): 2.5 days (1.8 to 3.2).

Why 2.5 and not 7.5 - 4.8 = 2.7? The Wilcoxon test comes with the Hodges-Lehmann difference: the median of all patient-to-patient differences, which is not the gap between the two medians.

Ask: which number goes in an abstract? Expected: the effect with its CI.
:::

## Worked example: reading the mortality comparison

::: {.neu-intro}
Question 1 (Q1) of the five FLUID-ICU questions: positive vs negative fluid balance by day 3, before adjusting for confounders.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Risks]{.neu-step-label}

- Positive: 134/373 = 35.9%
- Negative: 45/245 = 18.4%
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Difference]{.neu-step-label}

- 17.6 percentage points
- 95% CI 10.7 to 24.4
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Ratio]{.neu-step-label}

- Risk ratio (RR) 1.96
- About twice the risk
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Test]{.neu-step-label}

- Chi-square, p \< 0.001
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[But...]{.neu-step-label}

- Not adjusted for confounders: the positive group was sicker
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Report the effect and its CI. Then ask what else could explain it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Worked example (3 minutes): the Session 4 2x2 table on the dataset.

35.9% vs 18.4%: difference 17.6 points (10.7 to 24.4), RR 1.96, p \< 0.001.

But the positive group was sicker: the crude comparison cannot separate fluid from severity.

Model Results sentence: 'Twenty-eight-day mortality was 35.9% with a positive and 18.4% with a negative balance (risk difference 17.6 percentage points, 95% CI 10.7 to 24.4).'
:::

style="position:absolute;left:0.000%;top:89.535%;width:100.000%;height:9.302%;box-sizing:border-box;display:flex;flex-direction:column;justify-content:center;padding:calc(1.4 * 0.11292cqw);overflow:visible;text-align:center;align-items:stretch"><div style="font-size:calc(13 * 0.11292cqw);color:#8A99A3">r goes from -1 (perfect negative line) through 0 (no straight-line link) to +1 (perfect positive line)</div></div></div>
```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** r measures linear association, from -1 to +1. Always look at the plot.
:::

::: {.notes}
r summarises a scatter plot in one number, from -1 to +1.

The last panel is the trap: r near 0 but a strong curve. Always look at the plot.

With many patients a tiny r can be 'significant' and useless.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Linear regression: the model and how to read it

::: {.neu-intro}
You do not need to fit it. You need to know what each number means.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[When to use it]{.neu-card-title}

- The outcome is a number, e.g. PaO2/FiO2 ratio, ICU days
- Exposure: a number or a group
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[What the model looks like]{.neu-card-title}

- Outcome = a + B x exposure
- Adjusted: + B2 x confounder 2 ...
- A straight line through the data
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Its parameters]{.neu-card-title}

- a (intercept): outcome when exposure = 0
- B (slope): change in outcome per 1 unit of exposure
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[How to read B]{.neu-card-title}

- B = -15 per litre: each extra litre, the ratio is 15 points lower
- No effect: B = 0. Does the CI include 0?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Linear regression gives a difference (B) per unit of exposure, with its 95% CI. No effect = 0.
:::

::: {.notes}
The model in words first (2 minutes). Outcome = a + B x exposure. a is where the line starts, B is how steep it is.

Adjusting means adding confounders to the same equation: each B is then the change with the others held constant.

The next slide shows the line on data.

Ask: B = 0, what does the line look like? Expected: flat.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Slope = change in the outcome per unit of exposure. R² = how much the line explains.
:::

::: {.notes}
The model of the previous slide on simulated data. Intercept a = 292, slope B = -15 per litre. R² = how much the line explains.

Adding variables gives 'adjusted' slopes.

Ask: B = -15 (-19 to -11)? Expected: each extra litre goes with a P/F ratio about 15 lower.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Logistic regression: the model and how to read it

::: {.neu-intro}
Odds = probability / (1 - probability). A 20% risk is odds of 0.25.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[When to use it]{.neu-card-title}

- The outcome is yes or no, e.g. died by day 28, AKI
- Exposure: a number or a group
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[What the model looks like]{.neu-card-title}

- log(odds) = a + B x exposure
- Adjusted: + B2 x confounder 2 ...
- Gives an S-shaped curve of risk
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Its parameters]{.neu-card-title}

- B: change in log-odds per unit
- OR = e to the power B
- Papers report the OR, not B
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[How to read the OR]{.neu-card-title}

- OR 1.42 per mmol/L: odds of death 1.42 times higher per extra mmol/L
- No effect: OR = 1. Does the CI include 1?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Logistic regression gives an odds ratio (OR) per unit of exposure, with its 95% CI. No effect = 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
The model in words (2 minutes). It works on the log of the odds so that the predicted risk stays between 0 and 1: that is the S-curve on the next slide.

The paper reports OR = e to the power B. Above 1: higher odds. Below 1: lower odds.

Adjusted: confounders are added to the same equation, so each OR is for patients alike on the other variables.

Common mistake: 'OR 1.42 = 42% more deaths'. It is 42% higher odds.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Logistic regression turns a yes/no outcome into an odds ratio per unit of exposure.
:::

::: {.notes}
For yes/no outcomes the curve is an S. The model reports an OR per unit (here 1.42 per mmol/L lactate). Null 1.

Common mistake: 'OR 1.42 means 42% more deaths'. It is 42% higher odds.

Ask: what if lactate had no effect? Expected: a flat line, OR 1.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Which model? It depends on the outcome

| Your outcome is... | Model | The paper reports | 'No effect' value |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| A number, e.g. fluid balance (ml/kg) | Linear regression | Coefficient (B): a difference | 0 |
| Yes / no, e.g. died by day 28 | Logistic regression | Odds ratio (OR) | 1 |
| Time to event, e.g. time to death | Cox regression | Hazard ratio (HR) | 1 |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
The outcome type tells you the model and the number to read.
:::

::: {.notes}
The outcome decides the model: number, linear (difference, null 0). Yes/no, logistic (OR, null 1). Time to event, Cox (HR, null 1).

Common mistake: looking for 0 in an OR table.

Ask: length of stay as a number? Expected: linear, null 0.
:::

## What 'adjusted' means: compare like with like

difference</div></div></div>
```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Adjusting = comparing patients who are alike on the confounders.
:::

::: {.notes}
Crude: more fluid, more deaths (33% vs 18%). Split by severity: no difference in either stratum.

Severity drove both: confounding by indication. A model does this split for many confounders at once.

Only measured confounders can be adjusted for. Only randomisation handles the rest.
:::

## Reading a regression table, row by row

::: {.neu-intro}
Mock study of 600 ICU patients. One logistic regression model for death by day 28 with all five variables in it at once.
:::

| Variable | Adjusted OR | 95% CI | p-value | Does the CI include 1? |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| Positive fluid balance (yes vs no) | 1.80 | 1.20 to 2.70 | 0.004 | No |
| Age (per 10 years) | 1.25 | 1.10 to 1.42 | \< 0.001 | No |
| SOFA score (per 1 point) | 1.15 | 1.08 to 1.23 | \< 0.001 | No |
| Female (vs male) | 0.92 | 0.65 to 1.30 | 0.64 | Yes: compatible with no effect |
| Lactate (per 1 mmol/L) | 1.10 | 0.98 to 1.24 | 0.11 | Yes: compatible with no effect |

::: {.neu-table-caption}
Row 1 is the exposure of interest. Rows 2 to 5 are the confounders it is adjusted for. Each OR is adjusted for all the other rows. Read each row: comparison, effect, 95% CI, does the CI include 1?
:::

::: {.notes}
Read each row in four steps: the comparison (reference and unit), the effect, the CI, does the CI include 1?

OR 1.80 (1.20 to 2.70): 1.8 times the odds, adjusted.

Sex and lactate rows include 1: compatible with no association.

Mock data. Say 'associated', and 'odds', not 'risk'.
:::

## Check your understanding: read the regression table

::: {.neu-banner style="--c:#6C3483"}
QUICK QUIZ · 4 min
:::

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="60%"}
::: {.neu-activity-steps style="--c:#6C3483"}
- Go back to the regression table on the previous slide
- Poll: for female sex, does the 95% CI include 1? What does that mean?
- Poll: what does 'OR 1.15 per SOFA point' mean?
- Question for the class: one plain-language sentence for positive fluid balance
- Extra practice at home: Exercises 5 and 6 of the exercise sheet
:::
:::
::: {.column width="40%"}
::: {.neu-side .plain style="--c:#6C3483"}
The 4-step reading

- What is compared?
- How big is the effect?
- How wide is the CI?
- Does it cross 1 (or 0)?
:::
:::
::::

::: {.neu-output style="--c:#6C3483"}
**OUTPUT** One correct plain-language sentence, agreed by the class
:::

::: {.notes}
Check (4 minutes): go back one slide and keep the table on screen. Exercises 5 and 6 are homework. The answers are on the next slide.
:::

## Answers: read the regression table

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Female sex]{.neu-card-title}

- OR 0.92, 95% CI 0.65 to 1.30
- The CI includes 1
- Compatible with no association
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[OR 1.15 per SOFA point]{.neu-card-title}

- Each extra point: odds of death 1.15 times higher, adjusted
- Not '15% more deaths'
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Positive fluid balance]{.neu-card-title}

- After adjustment, about 1.8 times the odds of death by day 28 (OR 1.80, 95% CI 1.20 to 2.70)
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Say 'odds', say 'associated with', and always give the 95% CI.
:::

::: {.notes}
Answers (1 minute). Read the model sentence aloud. The table is mock data.
:::

## Overfitting: too many variables for too few events

:::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="38%"}
::: {.neu-side-notes}
### Why it matters

- The model learns the noise of these patients
- Effects too big, CIs too narrow
- It fails on new patients
- Flexible models, such as AI, overfit most easily
:::
:::

```

:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Plan about 10 events per variable. Choose variables in advance for clinical and biological reasons.
:::

::: {.notes}
Too many variables for too few events: the model learns the noise and fails on new patients. Flexible prediction models, such as machine learning, are the most exposed, but a regression with too many variables overfits too.

Rule of thumb: about 10 events per variable.

Choose the confounders in advance, for clinical knowledge and biological plausibility, and write them in the SAP.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Censored patients still count: they tell us they survived up to that day.
:::

::: {.notes}
A circle is a censored patient: followed until then, without the event. Censored is not excluded: they still tell us they were alive up to that day.

Ask: discharged home on day 9, never contacted again? Expected: censored at day 9.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Kaplan-Meier and the log-rank test: what they are

::: {.neu-intro}
Kaplan-Meier is not a model. It describes survival over time, using every patient, censored ones included.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[How the curve is built]{.neu-card-title}

- At 100% on day 0
- At each death it drops by the share who died among those still followed
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Censored patients]{.neu-card-title}

- Leave the count on their last day
- They are not deaths
- Shown as small ticks
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[What you read]{.neu-card-title}

- Probability of being alive on any day, e.g. day 28
- Median survival if it falls below 50%
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[Log-rank test]{.neu-card-title}

- H0: the two groups have the same survival over time
- Gives a p-value only, no effect size
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Kaplan-Meier shows survival over time. The log-rank test asks whether two curves differ. Neither adjusts for confounders.
:::

::: {.notes}
What Kaplan-Meier is (2 minutes). It is a way of counting, not a model: there are no parameters to estimate.

At each death the curve falls by deaths / patients still at risk. Censored patients leave the denominator without making the curve fall.

The log-rank test compares the whole curves and gives a p-value. To get the size of the difference, and to adjust, we need the Cox model (next slides).
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Read the steps, the ticks, the gap, and always the numbers at risk.
:::

::: {.notes}
Four reading steps: each step down is one or more deaths that day, ticks are censored patients, the gap is the difference, and the numbers at risk show how certain the right end is. The y-axis is the probability of being alive.

The log-rank test compares the two whole curves (H0: same survival). Here p = 0.040. It gives no effect size: that is the Cox model, next slide.

Ask: curves cross half-way? Expected: the effect changes over time.

Timing: 3 minutes.
:::

## Cox regression: the model and how to read it

::: {.neu-intro}
Hazard = the chance of the event at a given moment, among patients still at risk.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[When to use it]{.neu-card-title}

- Time-to-event outcome, e.g. time to death, with censoring
- To compare groups and adjust
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[What the model looks like]{.neu-card-title}

- hazard(t) = baseline hazard(t) x e to the power (B x exposure + ...)
- The baseline need not be specified
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Its parameters]{.neu-card-title}

- B per variable
- HR = e to the power B
- Papers report the HR
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#055F56"}
[How to read the HR]{.neu-card-title}

- HR 1.46: the death rate is about 1.5 times higher at any moment
- No effect: HR = 1. Does the CI include 1?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Cox regression gives a hazard ratio (HR), adjusted if confounders are added. It assumes the HR stays the same over time.
:::

::: {.notes}
The Cox model in words (2 minutes). It compares the rate of the event over time between groups, using censored patients too.

Each variable gets a B, reported as HR = e to the power B. Adding confounders gives an adjusted HR.

Its one assumption: proportional hazards, the HR is the same on day 2 and on day 20. Curves that cross suggest it does not hold.

We apply it to FLUID-ICU in 6.4.
:::

::: {.neu-big}
Adjust for what you planned, read the 95% confidence interval, and be honest about missing data.

6.4 Model the course dataset  \|  25 minutes

Section 6.4 (21:30-21:55): the models applied to FLUID-ICU. You will see confounding by indication shrink an odds ratio.

## The SAP came first

::: {.neu-intro}
The statistical analysis plan (SAP) was signed before the database was locked, i.e. before anyone looked at the data.
:::

:::: {.neu-steps}
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Primary outcome and analysis]{.neu-step-label}

- 28-day death
- Logistic regression, odds ratio (OR)
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Confounders]{.neu-step-label}

- Age, SOFA, lactate
- Vasopressor, ventilation
- Chronic kidney disease
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Supportive]{.neu-step-label}

- Kaplan-Meier and log-rank test
- Cox hazard ratio (HR)
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Subgroup]{.neu-step-label}

- One pre-specified: heart failure (yes/no)
:::
::: {.neu-step style="--c:#055F56"}
[Missing data]{.neu-step-label}

- Complete-case analysis
- Multiple imputation
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** All these choices were written down before anyone saw the results.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show the SAP on screen (SAP\_FLUID-ICU.md). Primary: logistic regression for 28-day death. Confounders chosen in advance. Kaplan-Meier and Cox as support. One subgroup. Complete case plus multiple imputation.

AKI and dialysis are not adjusted for: they come after the fluid.

Ask: why write this first? Expected: no one can say you chose the analysis with the best p-value.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Crude OR 2.49 shrinks to 1.62 after adjusting for the six confounders: still above 1.
:::

::: {.notes}
The key picture of the dataset (4 minutes).

Row 1: crude OR 2.49 (1.70 to 3.70) in all 618 patients. Row 2: the same crude OR in the 527 patients with complete data on all confounders: 2.22. Row 3: adjusted for the six SAP confounders (age, SOFA, lactate, vasopressor, ventilation, chronic kidney disease) in those 527: 1.62 (1.02 to 2.59), p = 0.044. Rows 2 and 3 use the same patients, so the drop from 2.22 to 1.62 is due to adjustment alone.

It shrank because sicker patients got more fluid and died more. What remains is modest and imprecise, and still an association.

Ask: adjust for AKI too? Expected: no, it comes after the fluid.
:::

**KEY MESSAGE** Read each row: comparison, OR, 95% CI, does it cross 1?
:::

::: {.notes}
The Q1 model as a forest plot (n = 527). One model with all seven variables in it at once, not seven separate models: each OR is adjusted for the other rows.

Row 1 is the exposure of interest: OR 1.62 (1.02 to 2.59). The other rows are the confounders: they are there to adjust, not to interpret.

Ask: which row goes in your abstract? Expected: only the exposure row, with its CI.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Day-28 survival 81.6% vs 64.1%, log-rank p \< 0.001: unadjusted.
:::

::: {.notes}
Read the real curve with the four steps. The shaded bands are the 95% CIs of each curve. There are no ticks because no one was lost before day 28: all survivors are censored at day 28. Most deaths are in the first week.

Day-28 survival 81.6% vs 64.1%, log-rank p \< 0.001, but unadjusted.

Ask: is the gap larger early or late? Expected: it opens early, then the curves run roughly parallel.
:::

## Cox model: the same story in hazard ratios

::: {.neu-intro}
The Cox model (6.3) applied to Q1, as a supportive analysis (04\_models.R). HR = hazard ratio. OR = odds ratio.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Crude HR]{.neu-card-title}

- 2.17
- 95% CI 1.55 to 3.05
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Adjusted HR]{.neu-card-title}

- 1.46
- 95% CI 1.00 to 2.13
- p = 0.053
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Check the assumption]{.neu-card-title}

- Is the HR the same over the 28 days?
- Test: p = 0.10, no sign it changes
- So the single HR is fine
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Compare]{.neu-card-title}

- Adjusted OR 1.62, p = 0.044
- Adjusted HR 1.46, p = 0.053
- Same direction and size
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** OR 1.62 and HR 1.46 point the same way with similar CIs. One p is just below 0.05, one just above: same conclusion.
:::

::: {.notes}
Cox adjusted HR 1.46 (1.00 to 2.13), p = 0.053. The proportional-hazards check asks whether the HR stays the same over the 28 days: p = 0.10 gives no sign that it changes.

The lesson: OR p = 0.044 and HR p = 0.053 tell the same story. Never let 0.05 decide what you believe.

Ask: how would you write this in the Results? Expected: both estimates with their CIs.
:::

## RR, OR and HR: what each means and when you meet it

::: {.neu-intro}
All three compare two groups. 1 = no difference. Above 1: more events. Below 1: fewer.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Risk ratio (RR)]{.neu-card-title}

- Risk in one group / risk in the other
- Design: trials and cohorts
- Analysis: a 2x2 table
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Odds ratio (OR)]{.neu-card-title}

- Odds in one group / odds in the other
- Design: case-control studies. Analysis: logistic regression
- Close to the RR when the outcome is rare
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Hazard ratio (HR)]{.neu-card-title}

- Event rate over time, one group vs the other
- Design: trials and cohorts with follow-up
- Analysis: Cox regression
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The outcome and the design decide the ratio: risk (RR), odds (OR) or rate over time (HR).
:::

::: {.notes}
RR: risks, from a 2x2 table (trials, cohorts). OR: odds, from case-control studies and logistic regression, close to the RR only when the outcome is rare. HR: event rates over time, from Cox.

Ask: Paper 2 compared deaths over time. Which ratio? Expected: HR.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** The reason data are missing decides how dangerous the gaps are.
:::

::: {.notes}
FLUID-ICU has missing lactate (Q4), so before handling it we ask why it is missing. Three mechanisms on the same 8 patients. MCAR: unrelated to the patient. MAR: depends on something recorded, here lactate was not measured for patients admitted at night, and we know who came at night, so multiple imputation can use that. MNAR: depends on the missing value itself, no method fully fixes it.

The data cannot prove which applies: write down why values are missing.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Lactate was missing mostly in less sick patients: not MCAR, but MAR is plausible.
:::

::: {.notes}
The bars show the share of patients without lactate in each SOFA band: 36% at SOFA 0-4, falling to 1% at 11 or more.

Lactate missing in 93 of 620 (15.0%), mostly in less sick patients (median SOFA 5 vs 8, mortality 19.4% vs 30.6%).

So not MCAR: complete cases drop the less sick. MAR is plausible, which suits multiple imputation.

Ask: why would lactate not be measured in the less sick?
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Multiple imputation keeps all 620 patients. The answer changes only modestly.
:::

::: {.notes}
A sensitivity analysis for missing data, here on Q4: the OR for death per 1 mmol/L lactate. Each model is run on complete cases (n = 527) and after multiple imputation (n = 620).

Unadjusted: 1.38 vs 1.44. Adjusted for age, sex and comorbidity: 1.39 vs 1.45. The third model adds SOFA on top of age, sex and comorbidity: 1.21 vs 1.23.

The conclusion does not depend on how missing lactate was handled.

Ask: how would you report this? Expected: both estimates, and that they were similar.
:::

## Exercise 8: answers (Q1)

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Crude]{.neu-card-title}

- OR 2.49 (95% CI 1.70 to 3.70)
- n = 618
- Table 6 of the Q1 pack
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Adjusted for the 6 SAP confounders]{.neu-card-title}

- OR 1.62 (95% CI 1.02 to 2.59)
- n = 527 complete cases
- The CI does not include 1
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Why it shrank]{.neu-card-title}

- Confounding by indication: sicker patients got more fluid and died more
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Part B]{.neu-card-title}

- Multiple imputation
- OR 1.70 (95% CI 1.09 to 2.64)
- n = 620, same conclusion
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** 'After adjustment, a positive balance was associated with higher odds of death by day 28 (OR 1.62, 95% CI 1.02 to 2.59).'
:::

::: {.notes}
Solution (1 minute). All numbers from Table 6 of the Q1 results pack (Table 3 has the same ORs). Read the crude sentence, then the adjusted one.

In Q1, Q2, Q3 and Q5 the adjusted estimate is closer to no effect. Q4 barely moves (1.38 to 1.39) until SOFA is added.
:::

## Proposal builder 6: what a good one contains

::: {.neu-intro}
Modelled on the running example (a restrictive fluids trial).
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Sample size]{.neu-card-title}

- Mortality 40% vs 30%
- Power 80%, alpha 5% two-sided
- 356 per group, 396 allowing for 10% loss
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Analysis plan]{.neu-card-title}

- Describe: n (%), median (IQR)
- Compare: chi-square
- Report: RR with 95% CI
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Confounders]{.neu-card-title}

- Chosen in advance
- About 10 events per variable
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Missing data]{.neu-card-title}

- Expected gaps and why
- Prevention
- How it will be reported
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Today: how many patients, which analysis, and what if data are missing.
:::

::: {.notes}
Show for 1 minute before modelling.

Sample size in one sentence with its four inputs and the drop-out allowance (356 per group, 396 with 10% loss).

Analysis plan in plain words, confounders in advance, a missing-data plan.

Each participant writes this for their own proposal.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra, Q2. AKI rises across balance groups: 29%, 54%, 63%, 75%. Adjusted OR 1.27 (1.16 to 1.40) per 10 ml/kg.

Caution: AKI can also cause a positive balance (reverse causation).
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra, Q3. Ventilator-free days pile up at 0 (death) and 28: report medians, use non-parametric tests.

Adjusted -0.61 days (-1.00 to -0.21) per 10 ml/kg.
:::

```

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A sample gives an estimate. The CI says how precise it is.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. The sample is the patients we study, the population everyone we want to learn about. 12 of 40 died: 30% (95% CI 17% to 47%).

Ask: 400 patients instead of 40? Expected: a narrower interval.
:::

## Extra: Reading a 95% CI in a real paper

::: {.neu-intro}
Paper 1 (Boulet 2024, pilot RCT), primary outcome: cumulative fluid balance at day 5.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[The result]{.neu-card-title}

- Median 6.9 vs 35.0 ml/kg
- Mean difference 13.2 ml/kg
- 95% CI -15.2 to 41.6
- p = 0.42
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Where is 0?]{.neu-card-title}

- 0 = no difference
- The CI includes 0
- So 'no difference' is compatible with the data
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[How wide?]{.neu-card-title}

- From 15 ml/kg in one direction to 42 ml/kg in the other
- Very imprecise: only 48 patients
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** 'Not significant' with a wide CI means 'we do not know', not 'no effect'.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Read every CI in three steps: the estimate, where the null is, how wide.

Paper 1: 13.2 ml/kg (-15.2 to 41.6), p = 0.42. Includes 0 and also a large difference: we do not know.

If asked why 13.2 is not 35.0 minus 6.9: it is a difference in means, the medians describe skewed data.
:::

:::

## Extra: Log-rank, Cox and proportional hazards

::: {.neu-intro}
Three terms you will meet in every survival paper. KM = Kaplan-Meier. HR = hazard ratio.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:3"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Log-rank test]{.neu-card-title}

- Compares whole KM curves
- Gives a p-value
- No effect size, no adjustment
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Cox regression]{.neu-card-title}

- Gives an HR with its 95% CI
- No effect = 1
- Can adjust for confounders
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Proportional hazards]{.neu-card-title}

- Assumes the HR is constant over time
- Crossing curves: be careful
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Paper 2 (Hyun 2023): Cox HR 2.13 (1.48-3.06), about double the hazard of death.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Log-rank: a p-value, no size, no adjustment. Cox: an adjusted HR with its CI. Proportional hazards: the HR is assumed constant, check it when curves cross.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Parallel lines: adjust. Different slopes: report the effect for each group.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Parallel lines: one adjusted effect is enough. Different slopes: interaction, report the effect in each group.

Pre-specify the few interactions you test, and test the interaction itself.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Find the null value first, then see if the CI crosses it.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Find the null first: 0 for differences (Paper 1 crosses it), 1 for ratios (Paper 2 day 2 is above it).

A CI that excludes the null means p \< 0.05, and the CI also gives size and precision.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** A good prediction model separates patients and gets the risks right, in new hospitals too.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Prediction models are judged by discrimination (AUC), calibration and external validation. A high AUC alone is not enough.

Ask: a vendor quotes AUC 0.92 in its own data. What do you ask?

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Extra: Prediction and machine learning: how to judge a model

::: {.neu-intro}
Machine learning (ML) is a flexible way to build prediction models. The same questions apply.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[What is it for?]{.neu-card-title}

- Predict an individual's risk
- Not to explain causes
- Who, when, which decision?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Enough data?]{.neu-card-title}

- ML needs many events
- Overfitting risk is high
- Internal validation done?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Does it work?]{.neu-card-title}

- Discrimination (AUC)
- Calibration plot
- External validation
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Is it reported?]{.neu-card-title}

- TRIPOD+AI checklist
- Code, data, fairness
- Impact on patients?
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** An AI score is a prediction model: ask for calibration and external validation.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Machine learning is prediction. Four questions: what is it for, enough data, does it work (AUC, calibration, external validation), is it reported (TRIPOD+AI)?

Accuracy is not the same as benefit.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Multiple imputation keeps every patient and admits the uncertainty of the gaps.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. Complete case: simple, loses patients, biased unless MCAR. Multiple imputation: fill each gap several times, analyse each, pool. It is honest about what we do not know.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::

## Extra: Report and test your missing data

::: {.neu-intro}
Four things a reviewer will look for. MI = multiple imputation.
:::

:::: {.neu-cards style="--n:4"}
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0D7377"}
[Report]{.neu-card-title}

- n missing per variable
- Flow diagram: who and why
- In Table 1 or a footnote
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0B376C"}
[Compare]{.neu-card-title}

- Patients with vs without complete data
- Are they different?
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#5FA39B"}
[Sensitivity (Level 3)]{.neu-card-title}

- Complete case vs MI
- Example script: 05\_missing.R
- Done hands-on in Level 3, Module H
:::
::: {.neu-card .plain style="--c:#0070C0"}
[Plan]{.neu-card-title}

- Write it in the SAP before you see the data
- Part 3 of your proposal
:::
::::

::: {.neu-takeaway}
**KEY MESSAGE** Missing data are a result: report them, handle them, test the answer.
:::

::: {.notes}
Extra. What a reviewer looks for: missing values reported per variable, patients with and without complete data compared, a sensitivity analysis, and a plan written in advance.

Timing: 2 minutes.
:::
